title: The Clausius-Clapeyron Equation
lead: Applied to a liquid and its vapor, the Clapeyron equation simplifies because the vapor takes up far more room than the liquid and behaves nearly as an ideal gas. The result ties how fast a vapor pressure rises with temperature to the enthalpy of vaporization.
objectives: Apply the Clausius-Clapeyron equation to estimate the vapor pressure at any temperature.
Estimate the heat of phase transition from the vapor pressures measured at two temperatures.

exercises.prompt: Show that the vapor pressure of ice at 274 K is higher than that of water at the same temperature. Note the curve of vaporization is also called the curve of vaporization.

answer.hint: Both curves pass through the triple point, 273.16 K and 4.58 Torr. Run the Clausius-Clapeyron equation from there to 274 K, with the heat of sublimation for ice and the heat of vaporization for water.
answer.solution:
Ice and liquid water have the same vapor pressure at the triple point, $\kTone = 273.16$ K and $\kPone = 4.58$ Torr. From there, $\ln(\kPtwo/\kPone) = -(\kDeltaHvap/\kR)(1/\kTtwo - 1/\kTone)$ with $\kTtwo = 274$ K, where $1/274 - 1/273.16 = -1.122\times10^{-5}$ K⁻¹. For water, with 45 051 J/mol, the exponent is $0.0608$ and $\kPtwo = 4.867$ Torr. For ice, the heat of sublimation is $6006 + 45\,051 = 51\,057$ J/mol, the exponent is $0.0689$ and $\kPtwo = 4.907$ Torr. Dividing the two,

$$ \dfrac{P_{ice}}{P_{water}} = \exp\left[\dfrac{6006\ \text{J/mol}}{8.314\ \text{J/(mol K)}}\left(\dfrac{1}{273.16\ \text{K}} - \dfrac{1}{274\ \text{K}}\right)\right] = 1.008 $$

so above the triple point ice has the higher vapor pressure. The sublimation curve is steeper because the heat of sublimation exceeds the heat of vaporization by the heat of fusion, and that is why ice above 273.16 K turns to liquid.

footnotes.html: $\kPone$ and $\kPtwo$ are both vapor pressures, the pressures of the vapor in equilibrium with the liquid at $\kTone$ and at $\kTtwo$.
The book prints this second example under the same number as the first, Example 23.4.1.
With the bracket rounded to $0.0032 - 0.0028 = 0.0004$ K⁻¹ the result would be 33.7 kJ/mol. The printed 39.0 kJ/mol comes from the unrounded difference, $1/313 - 1/351 = 3.459\times10^{-4}$ K⁻¹.
As printed, the sentence names the same curve twice. The curve for ice is the sublimation curve; the curve for water is the vaporization curve.
